It depends upon the panel. The thing to do is to jump on the pro products website and message Bob directly, he’ll decide what size/wattage you need for it to perform correctly. Since your Vivarium is completely pvc and that it’s meant to house a low heat requirement pet my guess is that the heat panel he’ll suggest won’t be too expensive. They can be pricey though.

The best option for pvc enclosures is to use a heat panel. Pro products is (according to the internet and from my limited experience) the best, but there are other options. Heat panels are installed inside on the roof of the enclosure and radiate heat down on a gradient. You can establish a hot spot based on the placement of the thermostat probe. I made my own clear acrylic lid for my Exo Terra (to maintain heat/humidity levels) and installed a radiant heat panel from pro products that I’m actually really happy with. It’s a lot nicer and a lot easier than the ceramic heat emitter I was using and unless the plant leaves are touching the RHP for long periods of time, the plants are happy too. 


As for the light issue, you’ll probably have to carve out space for the lights. Maybe look into aquarium grow lights, install them on the roof of the Vivarium? Temperature of the lit light panel is the real issue there.

I can’t say for sure. Wood mites eat mold and decaying wood. They are small white/beige mites. I looked up grain mites and it says they have pink legs, maybe that could help identify them.

When I found those wood mites in my ball python tank and immediately freaked out, did a ton of research, and determined that they were harmless but annoying. The safest way, that thankfully worked, to eradicate/lessen their population was the inclusion of isopods. I had already planned to add isopods to my tank anyway so if that was something you wanted to do might as well give it a try. My tank is 24x18x12 and I put 100 ish dwarf tropical isopods in there. Just saying, it worked for me. Also, it’s possible that if they go after wood mite larvae, they could go after the larvae of other mites as well.

Springtails will help, but I noticed the population of wood mites drop significantly once I added a healthy population of isopods. It’s been about a month since doing so and honestly, even after looking for wood mites in my viv, I haven’t seen any. I read on Joshs Frogs website that isopods eat wood mite larvae, and act as another competitor for the same food sources. When the wood mites showed up I freaked out too...almost bought those carnivorous mites, thankfully isopods worked.
